title: The termination certificate of the two-squares descent, read off the factorisation
statement: If m > 0, m*q = c*c + e*e, and both c and e lie in the symmetric band -m <= x + x <= m, then 0 <= q and q < m. This is the shape Fermat's descent actually consumes: it takes the FACTORISATION rather than the measure, and returns both halves of the termination argument at once.

formal.statement: theorem Int.descentMultiplierBounds : ((x0 : Int) -> ((x1 : Int) -> ((x2 : Int) -> ((x3 : Int) -> ((x4 : Int.lt Int.zero x0) -> ((x5 : Eq.{1} Int (Int.mul x0 x1) (Int.add (Int.mul x2 x2) (Int.mul x3 x3))) -> ((x6 : Int.le (Int.neg x0) (Int.add x2 x2)) -> ((x7 : Int.le (Int.add x2 x2) x0) -> ((x8 : Int.le (Int.neg x0) (Int.add x3 x3)) -> ((x9 : Int.le (Int.add x3 x3) x0) -> And (Int.le Int.zero x1) (Int.lt x1 x0)))))))))))

notes: 0 <= q because m*q is a sum of squares and m > 0 (Int.nonneg_of_mul_nonneg_left). q < m because (m*q)+(m*q) <= m*m is m*(q+q) <= m*m by Int.left_distrib, so q+q <= m after cancelling m (Int.le_of_mul_le_mul_left), and then Int.lt_of_add_le_of_nonneg finishes. Note the direction: nothing here divides c^2+e^2 by m -- q is a HYPOTHESIS, exactly as the quotients u and w are hypotheses of F:int-two-squares-descent-step, so the two compose without either one having to construct a quotient. Every bound here is spelled Int.add c c and NOT Int.mul (ofNat 2) c. The two are equal and the mul form reads closer to the textbook, but the add form is the one the existing shelf can MOVE: doubling an inequality is then literally Int.add_le_add h h, with no 0 <= 2 side condition and no numeral for ring::int to normalise. This is not a weakening -- 2*|c| <= m and -m <= c+c <= m are the same statement about c.
